questiontext.text: <p>Which four primary entity classes form the core foundation of computational information extraction and TEI Chapter 13 encoding?</p>

answer.text: <p>Persons, Places, Organizations, and Dates.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Computational entity recognition and TEI Chapter 13 standardize on people (<persName>), places (<placeName>), institutions (<orgName>), and calendar times (<date>).</p>

answer.text: <p>Nouns, Verbs, Adjectives, and Adverbs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are grammatical parts of speech, not named entity semantic categories.</p>

answer.text: <p>Parchment, Paper, Papyrus, and Vellum.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are historical writing materials and codicological substrates.</p>

answer.text: <p>Margins, Headers, Footers, and Columns.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are typographic and structural page layout elements.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Which TEI P5 XML element correctly tags the name of an official governmental institution or legislative body?</p>

answer.text: <p><orgName>Comité des décrets</orgName></p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. TEI P5 Chapter 13 designates <orgName> specifically for institutions, corporate bodies, and governmental organizations.</p>

answer.text: <p><institution name="Comité des décrets"/></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <institution> is not an inline named entity element in TEI P5.</p>

answer.text: <p><gov committee="yes">Comité des décrets</gov></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <gov> is not a valid TEI element.</p>

answer.text: <p><placeName>Comité des décrets</placeName></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <placeName> is reserved for geographic locations, not institutional bodies.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why must historical calendar dates be enriched with the @when attribute in TEI XML?</p>

answer.text: <p>To record a normalized, computer-readable date in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD) while preserving historical scribal wording in the text node.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The @when attribute bridges historical phrasing (e.g. 'the twenty-second Day of November') to standard machine-readable ISO dates (1752-11-22).</p>

answer.text: <p>To automatically delete the original scribal text from the electronic edition.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. TEI preserves the historical surface reading intact within the element.</p>

answer.text: <p>To tell the web browser to trigger an alarm clock on that calendar date.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. @when is an analytical scholarly attribute, not an alarm timer.</p>

answer.text: <p>To translate historical dates from English into modern Latin.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. ISO 8601 uses universal numerical notation, not Latin prose.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>What is the primary function of the @ref attribute on a named entity tag?</p>

answer.text: <p>To link the entity directly to a canonical URI in an external authority registry (such as Wikidata, VIAF, or GeoNames) or a local project identifier.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The @ref attribute establishes Linked Open Data connections to authoritative external registries or local prosopography.</p>

answer.text: <p>To assign a font size to the printed word on paper.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Font sizes are handled by CSS stylesheets, not @ref attributes.</p>

answer.text: <p>To count the total number of letters in the author's surname.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Character counting is not the purpose of entity linking.</p>

answer.text: <p>To indicate that the entity is a fictional character in a novel.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. @ref identifies real historical authority records regardless of genre.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>What protocol must an editor follow under our course rules when a historical person does not appear in Wikidata or VIAF?</p>

answer.text: <p>Document a Verified Absence by logging the searched repositories and dates, and mint a local project identifier (e.g. #person-001).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. When exhaustive searches confirm no external record exists, editors document the absence and create a local project identifier rather than inventing a link.</p>

answer.text: <p>Invent a synthetic 8-digit Wikidata Q-identifier and pretend it exists.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Inventing synthetic external IDs corrupts linked data integrity.</p>

answer.text: <p>Delete the individual entirely from the transcribed historical text.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Scholarly editions never alter primary texts to satisfy database limitations.</p>

answer.text: <p>Abort the editing project immediately and delete the repository.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Documenting verified absences locally is standard scholarly practice.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How do modern NLP libraries like SpaCy identify entity spans in unannotated running text?</p>

answer.text: <p>Using statistical sequence models trained on large annotated corpora to evaluate token transition probabilities and contextual embeddings.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Statistical NER models predict entity tags based on probabilistic contextual patterns learned from training data.</p>

answer.text: <p>By matching words against an alphabetical list of human names printed in 1850.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Static lists describe gazetteers; statistical models use contextual machine learning weights.</p>

answer.text: <p>By checking whether each word contains an even or odd number of letters.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Letter counts have no bearing on semantic entity recognition.</p>

answer.text: <p>By connecting directly to the human author via telepathic sensors.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Machine learning algorithms process digital textual data mathematically.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why do off-the-shelf modern NLP models frequently fail when applied to eighteenth-century archival manuscripts?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because modern models are trained on contemporary news and web text, making them fragile when encountering historical spelling, archaic punctuation, and early modern capitalization habits.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) mismatches occur when the orthographic patterns of archival witnesses diverge sharply from contemporary training data.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because eighteenth-century manuscripts are written in computer assembly code.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Archival documents are written in human natural languages.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because modern computers are legally prohibited from parsing texts written before 1900.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Software operates freely across all historical time periods.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because early modern printers did not use the Roman alphabet.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Early modern English and French used the Roman alphabet.</p>

name.text: 08 Question: Error Metrics: Precision and Recall

questiontext.text: <p>In named entity benchmarking, what does the Precision metric measure?</p>

answer.text: <p>The percentage of entities predicted by the automated model that were actually correct according to the human ground truth.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Precision = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives), measuring the accuracy of the model's positive claims.</p>

answer.text: <p>The percentage of all real ground-truth entities that the model managed to find.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. That is the definition of Recall, not Precision.</p>

answer.text: <p>The clock execution time required to process one manuscript page.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Processing time measures throughput, not mathematical accuracy.</p>

answer.text: <p>The number of words in the student's final analytical reflection.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Word count is an assignment parameter, not an algorithmic evaluation metric.</p>

name.text: 09 Question: Generative AI Hallucination in Entity Linking

questiontext.text: <p>What critical risk must scholars audit when using generative Large Language Models to link entities to external databases?</p>

answer.text: <p>The hallucination of plausible-sounding but completely fictitious Wikidata Q-identifiers or nonexistent authority URLs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Generative models prioritize fluent continuation and will generate syntactically convincing but fabricated identifiers if ungrounded.</p>

answer.text: <p>The physical corruption of the computer hard drive memory sectors.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Model inference does not physically damage disk sectors.</p>

answer.text: <p>The automated translation of all text into binary Morse code.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. LLMs output requested natural language or structured formats.</p>

answer.text: <p>The immediate deletion of the user's internet browser history.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. LLM inference does not manipulate local browser history files.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why does computational textual scholarship reject 'pure automation' in favor of a 'human-in-the-loop' paradigm?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because automated tools accelerate draft generation, but trained human scholars must audit, adjudicate ambiguous cruxes, and maintain ethical accountability for the edition.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Computational models lack historical understanding and accountability; human scholarly adjudication remains essential for authoritative critical editions.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because universities have banned all digital computers from humanities departments.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Universities actively champion digital humanities methodologies.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because automated models achieve 0% accuracy on every document genre.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Modern models achieve valuable accuracy, but their remaining errors represent critical historical cruxes.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because web browsers cannot display XML created by computer programs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Browsers parse XML regardless of how it was produced.</p>
